name: Respira Health: WhatsApp pulmonary rehabilitation in India (charityevals)
summary: Respira Health runs an eight-week pulmonary rehabilitation programme by WhatsApp chatbot, with physiotherapists on video calls, for adults in India who are breathless from COPD or other chronic lung disease. This model counts its first year (April 2025 to March 2026: scoping in India, a breathlessness education test and a pilot that enrolled 51 people) against that year's spending, and comes to {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000. Most of the year went on setting the programme up, so the cost per participant is high; the charity hopes to enrol about 1,000 people in its second year. Participants did about a third of the exercise sessions on average, and the pilot had no control group, so the gain in health is taken from studies of supervised rehabilitation and discounted for missing data. Its spending isn't published: the year's cost is our estimate from the money it raised and its budget.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Respira Health, digital pulmonary rehabilitation in India (April 2025 to March 2026)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Spending in the first year, April 2025 to March 2026 (our estimate)
rows.explainer: Respira Health publishes no accounts (it is a fiscally sponsored project of Anti Entropy, whose return doesn't show it separately), so the year's spending is judged from what it raised and planned. It raised $110,000 of seed funding in April 2025, which it called about half of its first-year budget, and $66,000 more by November 2025, when it said $23,000 more would let it finish the pilot with runway to June 2026: about $200,000 spent from April 2025 to June 2026, or about $170,000 over twelve months. From $130,000 (spending slower than raised) to $220,000 (the whole first-year budget). All of it counts: scoping, the education test, building the chatbot and running the pilot, with the founders' pay.

rows.label: Total spending in the first year (our estimate)
rows.explainer: One programme and no published split of management or fundraising, so total and programme spending are the same estimate.

rows.label: Programme spending in the first year (our estimate)
rows.explainer: As total spending: the overhead multiplier is 1, with the running costs inside the estimate.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
People enrolled in the pilot, January to April 2026

source.title: Respira Health, Digital pulmonary rehabilitation pilot report (single-arm, N = 51, January to April 2026; analysis dated 14 May 2026)

rows.explainer: Everyone the physiotherapists found eligible, even the 6 who never started (12%). The charity's own count from its chatbot records. How much of the programme they did is implementation_adj.

rows.label: Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: compare with the charity's own figure and with other models of the family.

rows.label: Years the gain from rehabilitation lasts
rows.explainer: Rehabilitation's gains fade over the following months without a maintenance programme, as follow-up studies report. A 2024 UK analysis of its health benefit, based on that literature, assumed the gain lasts 12 months and not beyond, given the variable preservation of quality-of-life gains after completion; with the fading, we take 9 months, from 5 to 12.

rows.label: Yearly death rate of the participants without the programme
rows.explainer: Adults with chronic lung disease, mean age 63, mostly mild to moderate (a baseline symptom score of 16 on the 40-point CAAT). Two anchors: India's life table (WHO, 2019) has 8.6% dying over five years at 60 to 64 and 13.3% at 65 to 69, about 2.3% a year, and chronic lung disease raises that; in a Kashmiri cohort after a hospital stay for COPD, 12.3% of the moderate (GOLD II) patients died within two years, about 6% a year, and 32% of all patients within one. These participants were recruited online, not after a hospital stay, so between the two: 4% a year, from 2% to 8%.

rows.label: Fall in the death rate with rehabilitation
rows.explainer: The reference class: in trials after a COPD exacerbation, rehabilitation went with about a third fewer deaths (Puhan et al. 2016, Cochrane: odds ratio 0.68, 0.28 to 1.67, 6 trials, low quality and not significant, the newer trials showing smaller effects); the 65 trials of rehabilitation in stable COPD (McCarthy et al. 2015) report no deaths outcome. These participants were recruited online with mostly mild to moderate symptoms, not after a hospital stay, so we take a third of the post-exacerbation fall: 10%, from almost none to 30%.

rows.label: Indirect deaths per direct death averted
rows.explainer: 0: the death rate above is from all causes.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Direct and indirect deaths over the years of protection. If the intervention protects several age groups with different risks, replace this formula with one row per group and sum them here; check the result against the all-cause trial result per person-year, scaled to today's mortality.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted under age five
rows.explainer: 0: the participants are adults.

rows.label: Share of the deaths at five or older that are aged 5-14
rows.explainer: 0: the participants are adults.

rows.label: Share of the deaths at 15 or older that are under 50
rows.explainer: Based on the participants' ages (mean 63, median 66, the pilot report's Table 1) and death rates that rise steeply with age (India's life table: 6% die over five years at 55 to 59, 13% at 65 to 69), few of the deaths averted are under 50: 5%, from 2% to 12%. The rest are valued at the site's weight for 50 and older.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: 0: the gain in health is counted directly in DALYs (dalys_illness_averted_per_person), never both.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per participant
rows.explainer: 0: adults with chronic lung disease.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per participant, ln(consumption) a year
rows.explainer: 0: the participants are mostly past working age, and no study measures an income gain from rehabilitation.

rows.label: Years until the income gain begins
rows.explainer: Not used: no income gain is counted (ln_income_gain_per_year is 0); the site's shared figure stays so the row means the same in every model.

rows.label: Years the long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, present value
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included, so the result moves with it. Never type in a present value worked out elsewhere: rebuild it from its inputs.

rows.label: Resource sharing within households (multiplier on an earner's gain)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household, so it counts this many times. Read by every model that values a long-term income gain (INV-13).

rows.label: Internal validity (both branches)
rows.explainer: 1: the before-after correction applies to the quality-of-life gain only and is in rh_before_after_adj; the deaths rest on a judgment anchored on randomised trials, already net of their control groups.

rows.label: External validity: supervised rehabilitation against a WhatsApp chatbot in India
rows.explainer: Delivery only (the participants' milder disease is in rh_milder_adj and mortality_reduction). Telerehabilitation did as well as centre-based rehabilitation on walking distance (mean difference 0.06 m, -10.8 to 10.9, 4 trials with 556 participants, moderate certainty; Cox et al. 2021, Cochrane), but those programmes were supervised live, mostly in high-income countries; this one is a chatbot with physiotherapists on call, in English and Hindi. 80%, from half to the same.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

rows.label: Share of the participants who wouldn't have had rehabilitation otherwise
rows.explainer: The participants came from Facebook and Instagram adverts across India, with no prior clinical relationship. Some hospitals in Indian cities refer patients to in-person rehabilitation (the charity found existing referral routes in many of the 12 it met), so a few might have had it anyway: 90%, from 75% to all.

rows.label: The charity's share of the resources behind the programme
rows.explainer: The charity pays for the chatbot, the adverts and the physiotherapists itself. Co-funders' resources are the volunteer clinicians who recorded content and advised (its website thanks a hospital respiratory team and several clinicians), at local clinicians' pay a few days' work, small beside about $170,000; Ambitious Impact, which incubated it, mobilised the charity and is no co-funder (normalization.md 2.24), and the participants' own time is no resource (Convention 2). 97%, from 90% to all.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Exercise sessions done per participant, on average

source.title: Respira Health, Digital pulmonary rehabilitation pilot report (single-arm, N = 51, January to April 2026; analysis dated 14 May 2026)

rows.explainer: The mean over all 51 enrolled, self-reported in WhatsApp and recorded by the chatbot (self-reports may run high; not adjusted, as the pilot's dose-response used the same records); 16 (31%) did at least 12 and a quarter did none or one.

rows.label: Exercise sessions in the full programme

source.title: Respira Health, Digital pulmonary rehabilitation pilot report (single-arm, N = 51, January to April 2026; analysis dated 14 May 2026)

rows.explainer: Three a week for eight weeks.

rows.label: Share of the full programme the participants did
rows.explainer: Sessions done over sessions planned: the gain is taken to grow with the dose, as the pilot found (sit-to-stand gains rose with sessions done, Spearman rho 0.69), so a participant doing a third of the sessions gets about a third of a full programme's gain.

rows.label: Funging and leverage
rows.explainer: Its funders (Ambitious Impact's seed grant and private donors) fund new charities; no government or other funder was paying for this work, so no money is displaced (1).

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: In November 2025 the charity held enough to run to about March 2026 and asked for more to reach June 2026: a few months' spending held, a quarter of a year, from none to half.

rows.label: From spending to the programme delivered
rows.explainer: 0: the spending is the year's running of the programme.

rows.label: Years from delivery to the middle of the protection
rows.explainer: The gain comes over the months it lasts, so it is discounted from their middle.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the benefits come
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit (the income gain's own wait is counted from delivery, in ln_income_gain_per_person).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the participants and the sessions they did are the charity's own count, but its pilot had no control group and measured no deaths, so the gain comes from studies of supervised rehabilitation delivered by others; the shared missing-data step applies. The charity plans a larger controlled study.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Treatment costs averted
rows.explainer: 0: a treatment programme; hospital stays it may avert are in other_unmodelled_share.

rows.label: Rebound
rows.explainer: 0: malaria prevention only.

rows.label: Investment of income gains
rows.explainer: 0: no income gain is counted.

rows.label: Other benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Fewer hospital stays for exacerbations and the families' costs of them (+3%, 0 to +10%: after an exacerbation rehabilitation cut readmissions, odds ratio 0.44, 0.21 to 0.91, but most participants are milder); the 2025 breathlessness education test, over 140 sign-ups of whom 18% finished a short course with no exercise (+3%, 0 to +8%); against it, injuries from exercising unsupervised (no severe adverse events in the pilot; -0.5%). Net +6%, from -3% to +20%.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: GiveWell-style supplementary adjustments, each its own row, summed: they add to the modelled value as one share, as in GiveWell's sheets.

rows.label: Deaths averted
Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the age band of each death averted (under five, 5–14, 15–49, 50 and over), times your multiplier on the value of a life: the site's one value of a death (docs/normalization.md 2.7).

rows.label: Units of value from deaths averted
Units of value from stillbirths averted
rows.explainer: A stillbirth averted at the site's one value (@givewell_shared.uov_per_stillbirth, GiveWell's), times your multiplier on the value of a life.

rows.label: Units of value from later-life income
Units of value from illness averted
rows.explainer: A share of the deaths' and income's value, the base GiveWell's supplementary share has.

rows.label: Gain in health-related quality of life after a full eight-week programme (EQ-5D-5L utility, 0 to 1)

source.title: Nolan et al. (2016), The EQ-5D-5L health status questionnaire in COPD: validity, responsiveness and minimum important difference, Thorax 71(6):493-500
source.page: Abstract, Results (324 patients with COPD, before and after 8 weeks of pulmonary rehabilitation)
source.quote: With rehabilitation, mean (95% CI) changes in utility index and EQ-VAS were 0.065 (0.047 to 0.083) and 8.6 (6.5 to 10.7), respectively

rows.explainer: The gain in health a full outpatient programme brings, on the 0-to-1 scale where a year at 1 is a year in full health, so a gain of this size held for a year is that many years of healthy life. A before-after measure (how far trials confirm it is internal_validity_adj); the gain for those who do part of the programme is implementation_adj.

rows.label: Share of the before-after quality-of-life gain that is rehabilitation's own
rows.explainer: The utility gain is measured before and after, without a control group, so it holds some recovery that would have come anyway and some regression to the mean. Randomised trials confirm a gain of similar size against usual care: health-related quality of life (St George's questionnaire) improved by 6.9 points (4.5 to 9.3) in 19 of the 65 trials of rehabilitation for stable COPD (1,146 participants; McCarthy et al. 2015), 5.2 in those at low risk of bias, against a minimum important difference of 4. So three quarters, from half to all of it. It applies to this branch only: the deaths branch rests on randomised trials.

rows.label: Quality-of-life gain of milder participants, relative to the study's
rows.explainer: Nolan's patients started with a COPD Assessment Test score of about 20; the pilot's participants started at 16.3 on the CAAT, with people with other chronic lung disease or breathlessness without a diagnosis among them, so they had less room to improve. The pilot's own pre-post changes point the same way as the trials (CAAT 4.4 points better, sit-to-stand 2.4 repetitions), but its general quality-of-life scores (EQ-5D-5L, Cantril ladder) didn't move in the 15 to 21 paired participants. 80%, from 60% to the same. The deaths branch takes milder disease into its own fall (mortality_reduction).

rows.label: Years of healthy life gained per participant, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The quality-of-life gain, corrected for the before-after design and the participants' milder disease, over the months it lasts, read as DALYs averted (the gain in a utility index stands for the fall in disability weight).

rows.label: Illness averted, in DALYs
Illness averted, in units of value
rows.explainer: The bridge from DALYs into units of value: the unit's conversion cancels it, so illness counts as healthy years whatever "Healthy year vs doubled-income year" is set to.

rows.label: Total units of value
rows.explainer: Illness and the other supplementary shares add to the modelled value side by side, as one sum of shares does in GiveWell's sheets; illness counted in DALYs comes in through its bridge, inside the side-effect share like every other outcome.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar
Staff pay as a share of the cost
rows.explainer: No accounts: the site's shared share for programmes where staff deliver the help (the founders and the physiotherapists who screen, assess and follow up each participant).

rows.label: Pay gap against comparable jobs
rows.explainer: The site's shared gap for health workers and field staff at nonprofits.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid by cash donations
Units of value per dollar you give
